claim: In 2017, approximately 1.8 million individuals became infected with HIV.
source: Recent global estimates suggest that in 2017 alone,~1.8 million individuals became infected with HIV giving rise to a total of 36.9 (31.1–43.9) million HIV-infected individuals (UNAIDS, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to UNAIDS 2017 report.

claim: In 2017, there were a total of 36.9 (31.1–43.9) million HIV-infected individuals globally.
source: Recent global estimates suggest that in 2017 alone,~1.8 million individuals became infected with HIV giving rise to a total of 36.9 (31.1–43.9) million HIV-infected individuals (UNAIDS, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to UNAIDS 2017 report.

claim: Progression to AIDS resulted in approximately 0.95 (0.67–1.3) million deaths worldwide in 2017.
source: Interestingly, despite an increase in the rates of accessibility to antiretroviral therapy (ART), progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) resulted in ~0.95 (0.67–1.3) million deaths worldwide in 2017 (UNAIDS, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to UNAIDS 2017 report.

claim: The risk of HIV transmission via rectal mucosa is approximately 10 times higher among individuals who practiced receptive anal intercourse than those engaged in vaginocervical intercourse.
source: Sexual intercourse is the primary route of viral entry, and the risk of transmission via rectal mucosa is reportedly ~10 times higher among individuals who practiced receptive anal intercourse than those engaged in vaginocervical intercourse (Hladik and McElrath, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hladik and McElrath, 2008.

claim: The enhanced susceptibility of colorectal mucosa to HIV infection is attributed to the structure and fragility of the epithelial layer as well as the activated nature of lymphocytes present in the colon.
source: The enhanced susceptibility of colorectal mucosa to HIV infection appears to be attributed to the structure and fragility of the epithelial layer as well as the activated nature of lymphocytes present in the colon (Elliott et al., 2018; McElrath et al., 2013; Grivel et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2018; McElrath et al., 2013; Grivel et al., 2010.

claim: Following introduction via semen, HIV breaches the rectal mucosal barrier either through ruptures caused during intercourse or via uptake by dendritic cells.
source: Following its introduction via semen, the virus breaches the rectal mucosal barrier either through ruptures caused during intercourse (Stax et al., 2015; Grivel et al., 2010), or via uptake by dendritic cells (DCs) (Grivel et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stax et al., 2015; Grivel et al., 2010.

claim: Pre-existing inflammatory conditions such as proctitis or infection by other pathogens such as HSV-2 and HPV could enhance the rates of mucosal susceptibility to HIV infection.
source: The presence of pre-existing inflammatory conditions such as proctitis (Bissessor et al., 2013) or infection by other pathogens such as Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) and human papillomavirus (HPV) (Freeman et al., 2006; Welling et al., 2015) could enhance the rates of mucosal susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bissessor et al., 2013; Freeman et al., 2006; Welling et al., 2015.

claim: DCs play a key role in HIV dissemination by mediating rapid HIV transfer to CD4+ T cells in the draining lymph nodes.
source: DCs play a key role in dissemination by mediating rapid HIV transfer to CD4+ T cells in the draining lymph nodes (McDonald, 2010; Preza et al., 2014; Saba et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McDonald, 2010; Preza et al., 2014; Saba et al., 2010.

claim: Host cell binding and incorporation of HIV is aided by different C-type lectin receptors, such as DC-SIGN, DCIR and MR expressed by DCs.
source: Host cell binding and incorporation of HIV is aided by different C-type lectin receptors, such as DC-SIGN, DCIR and MR expressed by DCs.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Infection of CD4+ T cells takes place through interaction between viral gp120 and T cell co-receptors such as CCR5 or CXCR4.
source: Subsequently, infection of CD4+ T cells takes place through interaction between viral gp120 and T cell co-receptors such as CCR5 or CXCR4.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about HIV infection mechanism.

claim: DCs can become infected with HIV although the level of infection varies with the DC subtype and maturation status.
source: Apart from transferring virions to bystander cells, DCs could also become infected with HIV although the level of infection varies with the DC subtype and maturation status (Bajtay et al., 2004; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bajtay et al., 2004; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2010.

claim: Tissue macrophages in colorectal mucosa function as key viral reservoirs.
source: Other antigen presenting cells like tissue macrophages in colorectal mucosa are also important from the disease point-of-view by functioning as key viral reservoirs (Brown and Mattapallil, 2014), not merely disseminating virus to T cells over a longer duration but also to DCs across mucosal tissues (Brown and Mattapallil, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown and Mattapallil, 2014.

claim: HIV triggers a local response in immune cells such as induction of IFN-γ, IL-12, TNF, IL-1β.
source: HIV, owing to its potential to activate several surface and cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, triggers a local response in immune cells such as induction of IFN-γ, IL-12, TNF, IL-1β (Sabado et al., 2010; McGowan et al., 2004) and the inflammatory levels appear to correlate with viral replication in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract (McGowan et al., 2004; Brenchley and Douek, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sabado et al., 2010; McGowan et al., 2004.

claim: Inflammatory levels appear to correlate with viral replication in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: HIV, owing to its potential to activate several surface and cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, triggers a local response in immune cells such as induction of IFN-γ, IL-12, TNF, IL-1β (Sabado et al., 2010; McGowan et al., 2004) and the inflammatory levels appear to correlate with viral replication in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract (McGowan et al., 2004; Brenchley and Douek, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McGowan et al., 2004; Brenchley and Douek, 2008.

claim: The severe depletion of intestinal CD4+ T cells that occur in the GI tract during HIV infection shifts their activation status from naïve to effector phenotypes.
source: Interestingly, the severe depletion of intestinal CD4+ T cells that occur in the GI tract during HIV infection shifts their activation status from naïve to effector phenotypes (Tanko et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tanko et al., 2018.

claim: The disruption in cellular homeostasis observed during the early stages of HIV infection is likely to contribute to immune activation.
source: Subsequently, the disruption in cellular homeostasis observed during the early stages of infection is likely to contribute to immune activation (Mehandru et al., 2004; Brenchley et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehandru et al., 2004; Brenchley et al., 2004.

claim: Th17 cells play a paramount role in maintaining mucosal immune responses against foreign invaders via secretion of inflammatory mediators, antimicrobial peptides and neutrophil recruitment.
source: Th17 cells play a paramount role in maintaining mucosal immune responses against foreign invaders via secretion of inflammatory mediators, antimicrobial peptides and neutrophil recruitment (O'Connor et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Connor et al., 2010.

claim: DCs exposed to complement opsonized HIV activate Th17 polarization in naïve T cells.
source: DCs exposed to complement opsonized HIV has been shown to activate Th17 polarization in naïve T cells (Wilflingseder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilflingseder et al., 2015.

claim: Th17 cells are characterized by the transcriptional expression of RORγt and secretion of IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22.
source: Characterized by the transcriptional expression of RORγt and secretion of IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22, Th17 cells are preferentially depleted during chronic HIV infection, a phenomenon directly linked to T-cell activation and HIV-DNA levels in the intestine (Klatt et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about Th17 cell characteristics.

claim: Th17 cells are preferentially depleted during chronic HIV infection, a phenomenon directly linked to T-cell activation and HIV-DNA levels in the intestine.
source: Characterized by the transcriptional expression of RORγt and secretion of IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22, Th17 cells are preferentially depleted during chronic HIV infection, a phenomenon directly linked to T-cell activation and HIV-DNA levels in the intestine (Klatt et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klatt et al., 2013a.

claim: Th1Th17 cells are positive for CXCR3 and CCR6, and express higher levels of both Tbet and RORγt.
source: More recently, another CD4+ T-cell subset Th1Th17, positive for CXCR3 and CCR6, as well as expressing higher levels of both T cell-associated transcription factor (Tbet) and RAR-related orphan receptor-γt (RORγt), has received attention owing to its likely role in HIV pathogenesis by serving as stable viral reservoirs despite the initiation of ART (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Th1Th17 cells serve as stable viral reservoirs despite the initiation of ART.
source: More recently, another CD4+ T-cell subset Th1Th17, positive for CXCR3 and CCR6, as well as expressing higher levels of both T cell-associated transcription factor (Tbet) and RAR-related orphan receptor-γt (RORγt), has received attention owing to its likely role in HIV pathogenesis by serving as stable viral reservoirs despite the initiation of ART (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: HIV infection can promote memory CD8+ T cell differentiation thereby augmenting the expansion of effector populations.
source: Together with its deteriorating effect on CD4+ T-cell subsets, HIV infection can also promote memory CD8+ T cell differentiation thereby augmenting the expansion of effector populations (Tanko et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tanko et al., 2018.

claim: The levels of activated CD8+ T cells expressing CD38 positively correlate with the amount of HIV RNA in the colon.
source: In addition, the levels of activated CD8+ T cells expressing CD38 have been reported to positively correlate with the amount of HIV RNA in the colon (Cassol et al., 2010; Crowell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cassol et al., 2010; Crowell et al., 2016.

claim: Tbet and EOMES regulate effector/memory functions of both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Both CD4+ as well as CD8+ T cells are under the regulation of T-box transcription factors, Tbet and Eomesodermin (EOMES) for defining their effector/memory functions (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: High frequencies of effector CD8+ T cells express Tbet and are often positive for EOMES.
source: It has been reported that high frequencies of effector CD8+ T cells express Tbet and are often positive for EOMES (Knox et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knox et al., 2014.

claim: Only a part of Tbet+ CD4+ effector T cells are Eomes co-positive.
source: To a certain extent, the situation is also similar to that reported in CD4+ T cells, although only a part of Tbet+ CD4+ effector T cells are Eomes co-positive (Knox et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knox et al., 2014.

claim: The expression of negative immune checkpoint molecules PD-1, TIM3, LAG3, and CD160 correlates with HIV viral load in the host.
source: On the other hand, the functional nature of these CD4+ or CD8+ T-cell subsets upon infection with HIV could be predicted from the expression of several negative immune checkpoint molecules, for instance PD-1, TIM3, LAG3, and CD160 (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Trautmann et al., 2006), which all correlate with HIV viral load in the host (Day et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Trautmann et al., 2006; Day et al., 2006.

claim: Elevated levels of CXCL10 (IP-10) in the peripheral blood during primary HIV infection is a sign of rapid disease progression.
source: Furthermore, the levels of cytokines and chemokines can serve as a measure of disease progression, for example, elevated levels of CXCL10 (IP-10) in the peripheral blood during primary HIV infection appears to be a sign of rapid disease progression (Ploquin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ploquin et al., 2016.

claim: Permissiveness to HIV infection by different CD4+ T-cell subsets is based on the differential expression of CXCR3, CCR4 and CCR6.
source: In fact, permissiveness to HIV infection by different CD4+ T-cell subsets based on the differential expression of CXCR3, CCR4 and CCR6 has been clearly elucidated (Gosselin et al., 2010; Gosselin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gosselin et al., 2010; Gosselin et al., 2017.

claim: Host defense includes the release of effector cytokines and lytic proteins, such as perforin and granzyme B by CD4+ as well as CD8+ T cells for killing virally infected cells.
source: Host defense also includes the release of effector cytokines and lytic proteins, such as perforin and granzyme B by CD4+ as well as CD8+ T cells for killing virally infected cells.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about host defense mechanisms.

claim: The initial host-HIV interaction includes the activation of complement system with all three cascade pathways.
source: Complement represents a key component of the innate defense armory and the initial host-HIV interaction also includes the activation of complement system with all three cascade pathways (Stoiber et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stoiber et al., 2008.

claim: Upon HIV infection, hydrolysis of C3 into C3b occurs on the viral surface, which sequentially becomes inactivated into iC3b.
source: Upon infection, hydrolysis of C3 into C3b occurs on the viral surface, which sequentially becomes inactivated into iC3b (Stoiber et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stoiber et al., 2008.

claim: The C1q pathway is activated and C1q fixation to the virions is especially efficient in the presence of HIV-1 gp120 and gp41 specific antibodies.
source: The C1q pathway is also activated and C1q fixation to the virions are especially efficient in the presence of HIV-1 gp120 and gp41 specific antibodies (Prohászka et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Prohászka et al., 1999.

claim: The virions transferred during sexual transmission via vaginal and rectal intercourse should be complement and/or complement antibody opsonized particles.
source: The virions transferred during sexual transmission via vaginal and rectal intercourse should be complement and/or complement antibody opsonized particles (Stoiber et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stoiber et al., 2008.

claim: Rectal mucosa houses CR3 (CD11b/CD18) on epithelial cells, DCs, and monocytes/macrophages, which have affinity towards iC3b.
source: Rectal mucosa is known to house CR3 (CD11b/CD18) on epithelial cells, DCs, and monocytes/macrophages, which have affinity towards iC3b as evident from studies using immune cells from blood (Bouhlal et al., 2001), a colorectal cell line (Bouhlal et al., 2002), or tissue biopsies (Hussain et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bouhlal et al., 2001; Bouhlal et al., 2002; Hussain et al., 1995.

claim: Complement-opsonized HIV is internalized more efficiently by DCs than free HIV.
source: Indeed, our previous observations have shown that not only were complement-opsonized HIV internalized more efficiently by DCs (Tjomsland et al., 2011), but also that opsonization decreased inflammatory and antiviral responses to enhance infection of immature DCs as compared to free HIV (Ellegård et al., 2015; Ellegård et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tjomsland et al., 2011.

claim: Complement opsonization decreased inflammatory and antiviral responses to enhance infection of immature DCs as compared to free HIV.
source: Indeed, our previous observations have shown that not only were complement-opsonized HIV internalized more efficiently by DCs (Tjomsland et al., 2011), but also that opsonization decreased inflammatory and antiviral responses to enhance infection of immature DCs as compared to free HIV (Ellegård et al., 2015; Ellegård et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ellegård et al., 2015; Ellegård et al., 2014.

claim: Free HIV activated higher antiviral responses in colorectal tissue compared to complement-opsonized virus initially.
source: Initially, there was higher antiviral responses in the free HIV compared to complement-opsonized virus.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The mucosal transcriptional response at 24 hr revealed the involvement of activated T cells.
source: The mucosal transcriptional response at 24 hr revealed the involvement of activated T cells, which was mirrored in cellular responses observed at 96 hr in isolated mucosal T cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: HIV exposure led to skewing of T cell phenotypes predominantly to inflammatory CD4+ T cells, that is Th17 and Th1Th17 subsets.
source: Further, HIV exposure led to skewing of T cell phenotypes predominantly to inflammatory CD4+ T cells, that is Th17 and Th1Th17 subsets.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: HIV exposure created an environment that altered the CD8+ T cell phenotype, especially when the virions were opsonized with complement factors.
source: Of note, HIV exposure created an environment that altered the CD8+ T cell phenotype, for example expression of regulatory factors, especially when the virions were opsonized with complement factors.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: HIV-opsonization alters the activation and signaling pathways in the colorectal mucosa, which promotes viral establishment by creating an environment that stimulates mucosal T cell activation and inflammatory Th cells.
source: Our findings suggest that HIV-opsonization alters the activation and signaling pathways in the colorectal mucosa, which promotes viral establishment by creating an environment that stimulates mucosal T cell activation and inflammatory Th cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a conclusion of the study.

claim: The number of significantly upregulated genes after 24 hr of HIV exposure was highest in F-HIV.
source: The number of significantly upregulated genes after 24 hr of HIV exposure, assessed in IPA, was highest in F-HIV, whereas when assessing 3-fold, 5-fold and 10-fold upregulated genes, the levels were similar across the study groups, that is F-HIV, C-HIV and complement and CI-HIV (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A showing gene expression analysis.

claim: Type I IFNs and antiviral and PRR pathways were highly upregulated in the colorectal mucosa following exposure to F-HIV but remained low or unaltered in the C-HIV-exposed tissues.
source: We found that an array of canonical pathways was affected by HIV exposure, and type I IFNs and antiviral and PRR pathways were highly upregulated in the colorectal mucosa following exposure to F-HIV but remained low or unaltered in the C-HIV-exposed tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing canonical pathway analysis.

claim: There was clear evidence of activation of IL-17-related pathways by F-HIV.
source: In addition, there was clear evidence of activation of IL-17-related pathways by F-HIV.
evidence: The claim is supported by the transcriptome analysis results.

claim: Complement opsonization of HIV led to the suppression of several T helper cell costimulatory signaling pathways.
source: Of note, complement opsonization of HIV led to the suppression of several T helper cell costimulatory signaling pathways (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing pathway analysis.

claim: Type I IFN signaling pathway was the major statistically significantly affected GO process in F-HIV.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis also revealed similar effects as the canonical pathways with type I IFN signaling pathway as the major statistically significantly affected GO process in F-HIV followed by protein folding, immune system processes, metabolism, response to stimuli and multi-organism process.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results.

claim: C-HIV significantly affected two major GO processes: modulation by host of viral genome and endoplasmic reticulum organization.
source: C-HIV significantly affected two major GO processes, which were modulation by host of viral genome and endoplasmic reticulum organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results.

claim: Immune response and regulation of locomotion were the main affected GO processes in CI-HIV-exposed mucosal tissues.
source: Immune response and regulation of locomotion were the main affected GO processes in CI-HIV-exposed mucosal tissues, and in addition ubiquitin-independent protein catabolism, SPR-dependent co-translational protein targeting to membrane, immune system process and MHC class II biosynthesis were also enriched processes (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis results presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Type I IFNs namely IFN-α1, IFN-λ and IFN-β1, P38 MAPK and IRF3 were significantly upregulated for F-HIV but remained unaffected in the C-HIV groups.
source: Next, we analyzed the upstream antiviral regulators assessing a heat map sorted by Z-Score and found a clear pattern with type I IFNs namely IFN-α1, IFN-λ and IFN-β1, P38 MAPK and IRF3 that were significantly upregulated for F-HIV but remained unaffected in the C-HIV groups (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by upstream regulator analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The inflammatory responses as measured by the expression of IL-1α, IL-1β and TNF were strongest for F-HIV but were also seen although at lower levels in the complement opsonized HIV groups.
source: The inflammatory responses as measured by the expression of IL-1α, IL-1β and TNF were strongest for F-HIV but were also seen although at lower levels in the complement opsonized HIV groups (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by upstream regulator analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The gene TGM2, activated by retinoic acid, was highly expressed across all the three HIV-exposed groups.
source: Of note, the gene TGM2, activated by retinoic acid, was highly expressed across all the three HIV-exposed groups (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by upstream regulator analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Interferon signaling, Th17 responses and markers of T-cell activation were factors separating the different HIV-exposed groups, with F-HIV resulting in a stronger activation of these responses than with C-HIV.
source: Furthermore, the top upstream regulators were divided into functional groups, and when a 3D PCA scatterplot was used to visualize clustering, we found evidence of interferon signaling, Th17 responses and markers of T-cell activation standing out as factors separating the different HIV-exposed groups, F-HIV resulted in a stronger activation of these responses than with C-HIV (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D PCA analysis presented in Figure 1E.

claim: At 24 hr, there were significantly increased levels of MXA (p=0.033), IFIT3 (p=0.0029), APOBEC3A (p=0.022), tetherin (p=0.012), SAMHD1 (p=0.022), and TREX (p=0.038) in F-HIV exposed mucosal cells as compared to unexposed cells.
source: At 24 hr, we found significantly increased levels of MXA (p=0.033), IFIT3 (p=0.0029), APOBEC3A (p=0.022), tetherin (p=0.012), SAMHD1 (p=0.022), and TREX (p=0.038) in F-HIV exposed mucosal cells as compared to unexposed cells (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Compared to F-HIV there were significantly lower levels in C-HIV and CI-HIV of IFIT3 (p=0.046, p=0.016) and SAMHD1 (p=0.036, p=0.039), and of TREX (p=0.015) in C-HIV exposed mucosal cells.
source: Compared to F-HIV there were significantly lower levels in C-HIV and CI-HIV of IFIT3 (p=0.046, p=0.016) and SAMHD1 (p=0.036, p=0.039), and of TREX (p=0.015) in C-HIV exposed mucosal cells (Figure 1 Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: APOBEC3A and tetherin transcripts were also upregulated for C-HIV and CI-HIV, with significantly higher levels for C-HIV of both APOBEC3A (p=0.022) and tetherin (p=0.0013), and CI-HIV for tetherin (p=0.008).
source: In addition, APOBEC3A and tetherin transcripts were also upregulated for C-HIV and CI-HIV, with significantly higher levels for C-HIV of both APOBEC3A (p=0.022) and tetherin (p=0.0013), and CI-HIV for tetherin (p=0.008) (Figure 1 Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Complement opsonization significantly increased HIV infection of emigrated mucosal DCs relative to F-HIV with a 2.9 fold increase for C-HIV (p=0.0156) and 2.6 fold increase for CI-HIV (p=0.017).
source: Complement opsonization significantly increased HIV infection of emigrated mucosal DCs relative to F-HIV with a 2.9 fold increase for C-HIV (p=0.0156) and 2.6 fold increase for CI-HIV (p=0.017) (Figure 2A), although no such effect was evident in the emigrated T cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The infection profiles of mucosal DCs isolated from the colorectal tissue matched the emigrated DCs, with complement opsonization giving rise to significantly higher levels of HIV infection with a 2.9 fold increase for C-HIV (p=0.0012) and 4.5 fold increase CI-HIV (p=0.0006).
source: The infection profiles of mucosal DCs isolated from the colorectal tissue matched the emigrated DCs, with complement opsonization giving rise to significantly higher levels of HIV infection with a 2.9 fold increase for C-HIV (p=0.0012) and 4.5 fold increase CI-HIV (p=0.0006) (Figure 2A,C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2A, C-D.

claim: The increase in infection by C-HIV with a two fold increase (p=0.009) and CI-HIV with a 1.95 fold increase (p=0.012) compared to F-HIV, was also seen for the CD163+ macrophages in the isolated mucosal immune cells.
source: The increase in infection by C-HIV with a two fold increase (p=0.009) and CI-HIV with a 1.95 fold increase (p=0.012) compared to F-HIV, was also seen for the CD163+ macrophages in the isolated mucosal immune cells (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2E-F.

claim: In the case of isolated mucosal CD4 T cells, complement opsonization did not result in statistically significant changes in HIV infection among the isolated mucosal CD4+ T cells as compared to F-HIV.
source: In the case of isolated mucosal CD4 T cells, complement opsonization did not result in statistically significant changes in HIV infection among the isolated mucosal CD4+ T cells as compared to F-HIV (Figure 2B,G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2B, G-H.

claim: The C-HIV and CI-HIV gave a significant fold increase in infection compared to F-HIV when pooling data from all infected immune cells (DCs, macrophages and CD4+ T cells).
source: To get an overall view of the infection profile of all infected immune cells, i.e. DCs, macrophages and CD4+ T cells, we pooled the data, analyzed, and found that the C-HIV and CI-HIV gave a significant fold increase in infection compared to F-HIV (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by pooled flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2I.

claim: The vast majority of isolated mock treated CD4+ T cells displayed effector memory phenotypes and the HIV exposure did not significantly alter the proportions of memory subsets.
source: The vast majority of isolated mock treated CD4+ T cells displayed effector memory phenotypes and the HIV exposure did not significantly alter the proportions of memory subsets (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Upon exposure to HIV (F-HIV, C-HIV and CI-HIV) the frequencies of naïve CD8+ T cells decreased from 8.2% for mock, to 6.7% for F-HIV, 2.3% (p=0.01) for C-HIV, and 3.9% (p=0.041) for CI-HIV.
source: However, upon exposure to HIV (F-HIV, C-HIV and CI-HIV) the frequencies of naïve CD8+ T cells decreased from 8.2% for mock, to 6.7% for F-HIV, 2.3% (p=0.01) for C-HIV, and 3.9% (p=0.041) for CI-HIV (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Tbet (mean 34.7% vs 19.5%, p=0.001), GATA3 (mean 49% vs 32%, p=0.007) and RORγt (mean 72.2% vs 46%, p=0.003) expressing CD4+ T cells were significantly increased in F-HIV-exposed cells compared to unexposed cells.
source: Tbet (mean 34.7% vs 19.5%, p=0.001), GATA3 (mean 49% vs 32%, p=0.007) and RORγt (mean 72.2% vs 46%, p=0.003) expressing CD4+ T cells were significantly increased in F-HIV-exposed cells compared to unexposed cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The levels of CD4+ T cells expressing RORγt or GATA3 remained unaffected by C-HIV exposure whereas the Tbet expression increased (mean 30.5% vs 19.5%, p=0.022), but to a lesser extent than F-HIV-exposure.
source: The levels of CD4+ T cells expressing RORγt or GATA3 remained unaffected by C-HIV exposure whereas the Tbet expression increased (mean 30.5% vs 19.5%, p=0.022), but to a lesser extent than F-HIV-exposure (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of RORγt+CD4+ T cells expressing Tbet increased significantly after exposure to F-HIV (mean 47.3% vs 35%, p=0.006), C-HIV (mean 57% vs 35%, p=0.001) and CI-HIV (mean 47.7% vs 35%, p=0.032) relative to unexposed cells.
source: The level of RORγt+CD4+ T cells expressing Tbet increased significantly after exposure to F-HIV (mean 47.3% vs 35%, p=0.006), C-HIV (mean 57% vs 35%, p=0.001) and CI-HIV (mean 47.7% vs 35%, p=0.032) relative to unexposed cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Within the CD8+ population there were a decline in frequencies of cells expressing Tbet or RORγt after exposure to C-HIV (Tbet mean 27.5% vs 38.6%, p=0.027 and RORγt mean 52.1% vs 68.5%, p=0.0019) and CI-HIV (Tbet mean 27.2% vs 38.6%, p=0.021 and RORγt mean 54.2% vs 68.5%, p=0.0076) compared to F-HIV.
source: Within the CD8+ population there were a decline in frequencies of cells expressing Tbet or RORγt after exposure to C-HIV (Tbet mean 27.5% vs 38.6%, p=0.027 and RORγt mean 52.1% vs 68.5%, p=0.0019) and CI-HIV (Tbet mean 27.2% vs 38.6%, p=0.021 and RORγt mean 54.2% vs 68.5%, p=0.0076) compared to F-HIV ('Figure 4C), whereas the expression levels of GATA3 and FoxP3 were not affected by any form of HIV exposure (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Complement opsonization of HIV and pathogens such as Francisella tularensis has the ability to initially suppress antiviral and inflammatory responses when targeting complement receptor three.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ellegård et al., 2015; Ellegård et al., 2014; Svanberg et al., in preparation; Dai et al., 2013.

claim: Opsonization of HIV alters the activation of signaling pathways and cells in the colorectal mucosa in a manner that promotes viral establishment and by creating an environment that stimulates mucosal T cell activation and inflammatory T helper cells.

evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.
